title: Body fat
what_it_is: Body fat is the share of your weight that is fat. The rest is muscle, bone and water.
green_text: Your body fat is within the expected range for your age and sex. That is a good place to be.
green_do: Keep up your strength work and your protein, so you stay lean without losing muscle.
amber_text: Your body fat is above the expected range. The good news is that body fat can change.
amber_do: Start with two 30-minute Zone 2 sessions a week and build towards three hours. Add two strength sessions, and a palm-sized portion of protein to every meal.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your body fat is well above the expected range. This is worth working on steadily, with support.
red_do: Let's build a plan together. Start with Zone 2 walking and simple strength work, and build up gradually.
low_text: Your body fat is lower than the expected range. That is common in people who train hard.
low_do: If this is not intentional, please mention it to your clinician. Please also mention it if you feel tired or have lost weight without trying.
info_text: Your body fat is a useful number to track over time.
info_do: We will look at it again at your next visit.
book: Zone 2 Training; Strength and Power; Nutrition
notes: Ranges: Gallagher 2000 (Table 4), by age and sex. Red = well above the 'overweight' limit. Edit the words freely.

title: BMI
what_it_is: BMI is a rough measure of whether your weight suits your height. It cannot tell muscle from fat.
green_text: Your weight suits your height. We read BMI alongside your body fat, because muscle is heavy too.
green_do: Keep doing what you are doing.
amber_text: Your weight is above the expected range for your height. BMI is only a rough guide, so we read it with your body fat.
amber_do: Look at your body fat result first. Then build towards three hours of Zone 2 a week and two strength sessions.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your BMI is well above the expected range. This is worth working on steadily.
red_do: Focus on steady habits: Zone 2 most days, two strength sessions a week, and enough protein. We can build a plan together.
low_text: A low BMI can mean there is little reserve if you become unwell.
low_do: If it is not intentional, or you have lost weight without trying, please mention it to your clinician.
info_headline: Read it with your body fat
info_text: Your BMI is above the expected range, but your body fat is within it. That can happen when someone carries a lot of muscle.
info_do: Your body fat is the better guide for you.
notes: Ranges: WHO adult groups. When BMI is high and body fat is healthy the app shows the grey 'read it with your body fat' version.

title: Visceral fat
what_it_is: Visceral fat is the fat stored deep inside your tummy, around your organs.
facts: Your visceral fat rating was {value}. On the Tanita's scale, 1 to 9 is healthy, 10 to 14 is high, and 15 or more is very high.
green_text: Your visceral fat is within the healthy band. That is good news for your heart and your metabolic health.
green_do: Keep up Zone 2, strength work and good sleep.
amber_text: Your visceral fat is in the Tanita's high band. It tends to respond well to regular exercise, better sleep and less alcohol.
amber_do: Build towards three hours of Zone 2 a week. Keep alcohol to 14 units or fewer, and favour whole foods.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your visceral fat is in the Tanita's very high band. Bringing it down is one of the most useful things you can do for your heart and metabolic health.
red_do: Build towards three hours of Zone 2 and two strength sessions a week. Keep alcohol to 14 units or fewer, and talk it through with your clinician.
notes: Tanita MC-780MA professional bands, as drawn on the printed report: 1-9 healthy, 10-14 high, 15 and above very high. Checked on 2026-10-19 against a printed report where a level of 12 is drawn in the High band. The PDF reader also reads which band the bar is drawn in and warns the clinician if it ever disagrees.

title: Muscle balance, left and right
what_it_is: This compares the muscle in your left and right arms, and your left and right legs, from your Tanita.
green_text: The muscle on your left and right sides is well matched.
amber_text: One side has less muscle than the other, or the Tanita marks a limb outside its normal range. This is common and usually responds well to training.
amber_do: Add single-leg and single-arm exercises, and start each set with your weaker side. We will check your balance again at your next visit.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: One side has much less muscle than the other. It is worth finding out why, for example an old injury or favouring one side.
red_do: Talk this through with your clinician, who can plan exercises for your weaker side.
notes: Rule 'limbs': the difference between the two sides as a % of the bigger side. Green under 10%, amber 10 to 19.9%, red 20% or more. A limb the Tanita itself marks outside normal (orange bar, the Limb Flags box) makes it at least amber. The 10% and 20% cut-offs are the clinic's own working guide, not a published standard: change them here if you prefer others.

title: Leg muscle score
what_it_is: Your Tanita scores the muscle in your legs against your body weight. Its chart shows the score expected for your age as a line.
green_text: Your leg muscle score is at or above the line for your age. Strong legs help you stay active and steady on your feet.
green_do: Keep up your leg strength work, such as squats, step-ups and walking uphill.
amber_text: Your leg muscle score is below the line for your age. Leg muscle responds well to regular strength work at any age.
amber_do: Add two leg strength sessions a week, such as sit-to-stands, step-ups and squats. Eat some protein at every meal.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your leg muscle score is well below the line for your age.
red_do: Talk this through with your clinician, who can plan safe leg strength work for you.
info_text: Your clinician will go through where your score sits on the Tanita's chart with you.
notes: Rule 'zone': the light is the colour of the Tanita chart around the score (green above the age line, orange below), read from the PDF or entered in the 'Leg Muscle Score Zone' box. Green gives green, orange gives amber; red is not used. Without a colour the tile is grey. Check the definition of the score against Tanita's documentation before approving.

title: Phase angle
what_it_is: Phase angle reflects the health of your body's cells and the quality of your muscle.
facts: Your phase angle was {value}. The Tanita marks 7 degrees or more as healthy.
green_text: Your phase angle is in the healthy band. That suggests your muscle and cells are in good condition.
green_do: Keep up your strength training and your protein.
amber_text: Your phase angle is below the healthy mark. It tends to improve with strength training, enough protein and good sleep.
amber_do: Add two strength sessions a week, with a palm-sized portion of protein at every meal. We will check it again at your next visit.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your phase angle is low. This is worth talking through with your clinician.
red_do: Please book a conversation. Meanwhile, start gentle strength work and make sure you eat enough protein.
notes: From the bands printed on the Tanita report: 7 degrees healthy (7-12 athletic), 5 in-risk/ageing, 2 severely malnourished. Green 7+, amber 5 to under 7, red under 5.

title: Phase angle in your arms and legs
what_it_is: The Tanita also measures phase angle in each arm and leg. It shows where your muscle quality is strongest and where it could improve.
members: Right Arm Phase Angle|Left Arm Phase Angle|Right Leg Phase Angle|Left Leg Phase Angle
facts: The Tanita marks 7 degrees or more as healthy, and 5 degrees as in-risk or ageing.
green_text: Your arms and legs are all in the healthy band.
green_do: Keep up your strength training and your protein.
amber_text: At least one arm or leg is below the healthy mark. Phase angle tends to improve with strength training, enough protein and good sleep.
amber_do: Strength train the arms or legs marked below the mark twice a week, with protein at every meal. We will check again at your next visit.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: At least one arm or leg has a low phase angle. This is worth talking through with your clinician.
red_do: Please book a conversation. Meanwhile, start gentle strength work and make sure you eat enough protein.
notes: Rule 'parts': the same bands as the whole-body phase angle row (from the Tanita report: 7 healthy, 5 in-risk/ageing). Green 7+, amber 5 to under 7, red under 5, for each limb; the tile shows the worst.

title: Muscle mass
what_it_is: This is the total weight of muscle in your body, including your trunk, arms and legs.
green_text: Your muscle mass is in the Tanita's normal range or above for your age, sex and height.
green_do: Keep strength training at least twice a week and eat enough protein. We will compare your muscle at each visit.
amber_text: Your muscle mass is below the Tanita's normal range for your age, sex and height. Muscle responds well to strength training and protein at any age.
amber_do: Strength train at least twice a week, and have a palm-sized portion of protein at every meal. We will compare your muscle at each visit.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your muscle mass is well below the Tanita's normal range.
red_do: Talk this through with your clinician, who can plan safe strength work and check your protein.
info_text: There is no single right number, because it depends on your size, age and sex. What matters is the direction over time.
info_do: Keep strength training at least twice a week and eat enough protein. We will compare your muscle at each visit.
notes: Rule 'zone': the light comes from the band the Tanita draws the muscle mass bar in (Low, Normal or High, for the person's age, sex and height), read from the PDF or entered in the 'Muscle Mass Band' box. Normal or High gives green, Low gives amber; red is not used. With no band the tile is grey, as before.

title: Arm and leg muscle (sarcopenia check)
what_it_is: This adds up the muscle in your arms and legs and compares it with your height. It is how doctors in Europe check for low muscle.
green_text: Your arm and leg muscle is above the line the European guidance uses for low muscle.
green_do: Keep strength training at least twice a week and eat enough protein to hold on to it.
amber_text: Your arm and leg muscle is under the line the European guidance uses for low muscle. Your clinician will look at it together with your strength results.
amber_do: Strength train at least twice a week, and have a palm-sized portion of protein at every meal. We will check again at your next visit.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your arm and leg muscle is well under the line for low muscle.
red_do: Talk this through with your clinician, who can plan safe strength work and check your protein.
low_text: Your arm and leg muscle is under the line the European guidance uses for low muscle. Your clinician will look at it together with your strength results.
low_do: Strength train at least twice a week, and have a palm-sized portion of protein at every meal. We will check again at your next visit.
notes: Engine result asm_index: the four Tanita limb muscle values added together, divided by height squared (the clinician's height, or the Tanita's). EWGSOP2 2019 Table 3: low under 7.0 kg/m2 for men and 5.5 for women (or under 20 kg / 15 kg with no height). A body composition scale is a guide: the cut-offs come mainly from DXA. Needs the participant's sex.

title: Metabolic age
what_it_is: Metabolic age is the age the Tanita estimates your body composition matches.
info_text: It is a rough guide and not a medical measure. Compare it with your real age and watch the trend.
info_do: Strength, Zone 2 and good sleep all help.
notes: Shown as information only. It can be given a light later if you want one.

title: Skin AGE level
what_it_is: AGEs are substances that build up in your skin as you age. The AGE Reader measures them painlessly through your skin.
green_text: Your skin AGE level is a good sign for someone your age.
green_do: Keep going. Whole foods, regular exercise and not smoking all help to keep AGEs down.
amber_text: Your skin AGE level is a little high for your age.
amber_do: Look at your sleep, activity and food. Regular exercise and a whole-food diet can help.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: The AGE Reader has flagged this result. Your clinician will talk through what it means for you.
red_do: Please book a conversation. A GP check of your blood sugar and blood pressure is a sensible next step.
info_text: Your skin AGE level is higher than the average for your age. AGEs build up with high blood sugar, smoking and some highly processed or heavily browned foods.
info_do: Look at your sleep, activity and food. We will track it at your next visit.
notes: Uses the AGE Reader's own norms: the average for your age and its own label. Lower than average is good. A label of moderate, medium, high or increased risk shows red.

title: Skin age estimate (BodyAge)
what_it_is: BodyAge is the age at which an average person has your skin AGE level, according to the AGE Reader.
green_text: Your skin looks younger than your age on this measure. It is the device's own estimate, so treat it as a guide.
green_do: Keep doing what you are doing.
amber_text: Your BodyAge is older than your age. It is the device's own estimate, so treat it as a guide.
amber_do: Sleep, activity and food all play a part. We will track it at your next visit.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your BodyAge is well above your age. It is the device's own estimate, so treat it as a guide.
red_do: Please book a conversation so we can look at the bigger picture.
info_text: Your BodyAge is older than your age. It is the device's own estimate, so treat it as a guide.
info_do: Sleep, activity and food all play a part. We will track it at your next visit.
notes: The device's own estimate. Younger or the same shows green; older shows grey (information).

title: Heart rate (at your ECG)
what_it_is: This is how many times your heart beat each minute during your ECG recording.
green_text: Your heart rate was within the expected range for your age and sex. A lower resting heart rate usually goes with better fitness.
green_do: Keep up your Zone 2 training. It is the best way to keep your resting heart rate down.
amber_text: Your heart rate is at the edge of the expected range.
amber_do: We will check it again at your next visit.
red_text: Your heart rate was outside the expected range. There are often harmless reasons, such as nerves, caffeine or being very fit.
red_do: Please talk it through with your clinician. If you ever have chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness or palpitations, stop and seek medical help.
low_text: Your heart rate was lower than the expected range. That is common in people who train regularly.
low_do: If you also feel dizzy, faint or breathless, speak to your clinician or GP.
info_text: Your heart rate at your ECG is a useful number to track.
info_do: We will look at it again at your next visit.
notes: Ranges: Rijnbeek 2014, by age and sex. The wording of 'outside the range' is deliberately not a diagnosis.

title: Heart electrical timings
what_it_is: These timings show how quickly the electrical signal moves through your heart and resets between beats.
green_text: All your heart timings are within the expected range for your age and sex. That is reassuring.
green_do: Nothing to do here. Keep up your regular activity.
amber_text: One of your heart timings is close to the edge of the expected range.
amber_do: We will check it again at your next visit.
red_text: One or more of your heart timings is outside the expected range. There are often harmless explanations.
red_do: Please talk it through with your clinician. If you ever have chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness or palpitations, stop and seek medical help.
notes: The light is the worst of the three timings (PR interval, QRS duration and QTc). QTc uses the Fridericia correction.

title: Blood oxygen
what_it_is: This is how much oxygen your blood is carrying, as a percentage.
green_text: Your blood oxygen was within the expected range. That is a good sign that your heart and lungs are working well together.
green_do: Keep up your Zone 2 training. It helps your body use oxygen well.
amber_text: Your blood oxygen is close to the edge of the expected range.
amber_do: We may repeat it at your next visit.
red_text: Your blood oxygen was lower than the expected range. A short reading can be affected by cold hands, movement or nail polish.
red_do: We may repeat it. If you feel breathless, speak to your clinician or GP.
notes: Under 65: 95% or above. 65 and over: 91% or above. Only shows if a pulse oximeter was used.

title: Resting pulse
what_it_is: Your pulse is how many times your heart beats each minute while you are at rest.
green_text: Your resting pulse is within the expected range for your age and sex. A lower resting pulse usually goes with better fitness.
green_do: Zone 2 is the best way to bring it down further. Start with two 30-minute sessions a week and build up.
amber_text: Your resting pulse is above the expected range. Caffeine, poor sleep, stress and being less fit can all raise it.
amber_do: Build towards three hours of Zone 2 a week, protect your sleep, and keep caffeine to the morning.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your resting pulse is well outside the expected range. Please talk it through with your clinician.
red_do: If you ever feel dizzy, faint or breathless, speak to your clinician or GP.
low_text: Your resting pulse is lower than the expected range. That is common in people who exercise regularly.
low_do: If you also feel dizzy, faint or breathless, speak to your clinician or GP.
info_text: Your resting pulse is a useful number to track over time.
info_do: We will look at it again at your next visit.
notes: Ranges: NHANES (US health survey), by age and sex. Your booklet's scorecard uses under 65 / 65 to 80 / over 80. Tell me if you want those instead.

title: Left and right sides
what_it_is: The force plates measure each leg on its own. This shows whether one side is doing less of the work.
green_text: Your left and right sides shared the work evenly in these tests.
amber_text: One side did noticeably less of the work in at least one test. This is common and usually responds well to training the weaker side.
amber_do: Add single-leg exercises such as split squats and step-ups, and start each set with your weaker side. We will check again at your next visit.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: One side did much less of the work in at least one test. It is worth finding out why, for example an old injury or pain.
red_do: Talk this through with your clinician, who can plan exercises for your weaker side.
notes: Rule 'fp_balance': VALD asymmetry from sit-to-stand, squat and jump (VALD's letter = the side that produced more, so the other side is weaker; checked against the force traces of a squat report on 2026-10-19), plus single-leg stance sway velocity left vs right. Green under 10%, amber 10 to 19.9%, red 20% or more: the clinic's own working guide. The 2021 systematic review (Parkinson et al.) found 10-15% cut-offs are common but weakly supported, so compare each person with their own earlier results too.

title: Strength compared with people your age
what_it_is: VALD compares your force plate results with people of your age and sex. The 50th percentile is average.
facts: The 25th percentile means you scored higher than 25 in every 100 people of your age and sex.
green_text: Your strength is in the usual range or better for your age and sex.
green_do: Keep up your strength training two or three times a week.
amber_text: At least one result is lower than most people of your age and sex. Strength responds well to training at any age.
amber_do: Add two strength sessions a week for your legs, such as sit-to-stands, squats and step-ups.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: At least one result is well below most people of your age and sex.
red_do: Talk this through with your clinician, who can plan a safe strength programme for you.
notes: Rule 'parts' across tests: the percentile the clinician copies from VALD Hub for each test (CMJ: jump height or peak power per kg; squat: peak force; sit-to-stand: peak standing force). Green 25th percentile or above, amber 10th to 24th, red below the 10th: the clinic's own choice. Squat and sit-to-stand force are also shown as times body weight when the body weight is entered.

title: Fitness (estimated VO2 max)
what_it_is: VO2 max is how much oxygen your body can use at full effort. Here it is estimated from your activity level, age, sex and body fat.
green_text: Your estimated fitness is in the usual range or better for your age and sex. Fitness is one of the strongest signs of long-term health.
green_do: Keep up your Zone 2 work, and add one harder session a week to push it higher.
amber_text: Your estimated fitness is lower than most people of your age and sex. Fitness responds well to regular aerobic exercise at any age.
amber_do: Build towards three hours of Zone 2 a week, such as brisk walking or easy cycling. Add one harder session once that feels easy.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your estimated fitness is lower than almost everyone of your age and sex. Building it up is one of the best things you can do for your health.
red_do: Start gently, with short brisk walks most days, and build up week by week. Your clinician will plan this with you.
low_text: Your estimated fitness is lower than most people of your age and sex. Fitness responds well to regular aerobic exercise at any age.
low_do: Build towards three hours of Zone 2 a week, such as brisk walking or easy cycling. Add one harder session once that feels easy.
notes: Engine result vo2max_est: Jackson 1990 non-exercise model, VO2max = 50.513 + 1.589 x activity rating (0-7) - 0.289 x age - 0.522 x body fat % + 5.863 for men (or the BMI model, 56.363 + 1.921 x rating - 0.381 x age - 0.754 x BMI + 10.987 for men, when there is no body fat), placed on the FRIEND 2015 treadmill percentiles for age and sex. Green 25th percentile and above, amber 5th to 25th, red under the 5th. Needs the activity rating (the 'Physical Activity Rating (PA-R)' assessment). An estimate: a measured test (treadmill or bike with gas analysis) is better.

title: Longevity age (estimate)
what_it_is: The average of the age your Tanita estimates for your body and the age your AGE Reader estimates for your skin.
green_text: Your devices put your body at or below your actual age. It is a simple average, not a medical test, but it is a good sign.
green_do: Keep doing what you are doing. We will follow this number at each visit.
amber_text: Your devices put your body a little older than your actual age. Strength, fitness, sleep and food all move these numbers.
amber_do: Start with the top things to work on, above. We will follow this number at each visit.
red_headline: A good place to focus first
red_text: Your devices put your body well above your actual age. Strength, fitness, sleep and food all move these numbers.
red_do: Start with the top things to work on, above, and talk through a plan with your clinician.
book: Zone 2 Training; Strength and Power; Nutrition; Sleep
notes: Engine result longevity_age: the average of the Tanita's metabolic age and the AGE Reader's BodyAge, compared with the actual age. Green at or below the actual age, amber above it. Only shown when both are entered. A summary to track, not a validated measure of biological ageing.
